name: Vitamin D3 + K2
what: Vitamin D3 paired with vitamin K2, usually as a softgel or drops.
why: Supports normal immune function and bone health, especially in winter or when you get little sun.*

evidence.note: Pooled trials found a small drop in respiratory infections with daily vitamin D. The effect is modest and clearest in people who start out low.

caution: Vitamin K can interfere with warfarin and other blood thinners. Very high doses of vitamin D can raise blood calcium. Ask your doctor if you take thiazide diuretics or have kidney disease.

name: Vitamin C
what: An essential vitamin, sold as capsules, powder or chewables.
why: Supports immune cell function. Taken regularly, it may help shorten colds a little.*

evidence.note: A Cochrane review found regular vitamin C did not reduce how often most people catch colds, but shortened them by about 8% in adults. Starting after symptoms begin showed no consistent benefit.

caution: Doses above 2,000 mg a day can cause stomach upset and diarrhea. Check with your doctor if you have a history of kidney stones or iron overload (hemochromatosis).

name: Zinc
what: An essential mineral, sold as capsules or tablets (often zinc picolinate or gluconate).
why: Supports normal immune function, especially if your diet is low in zinc.*

evidence.note: Zinc is needed for immune cells to work normally. Cochrane found no clear evidence that daily zinc reduces the number of colds people catch.

caution: Stay under 40 mg a day unless your doctor says otherwise. Long-term high doses can lower copper levels. Take it a few hours apart from antibiotics and penicillamine.

name: Quercetin
what: A plant flavonoid found in onions, apples and berries, sold as tablets or capsules.
why: Used for antioxidant support and to support immune and respiratory health.*

evidence.note: The largest trial (1,002 adults, 12 weeks) found no overall effect on upper respiratory illness. A benefit appeared only in one subgroup, so it needs confirming.
evidence.label: Early research

caution: Can interact with some antibiotics, blood thinners and blood pressure medicines. Not well studied in pregnancy or breastfeeding. High doses may be hard on the kidneys.

name: Aged Garlic Extract
what: Garlic that has been aged to mellow the odor, sold as capsules.
why: Supports immune cell function. People take it daily through the winter.*

evidence.note: One trial of 146 people reported fewer colds with a garlic supplement, and one trial of aged garlic extract showed changes in immune cells. Cochrane says more trials are needed.

caution: Garlic can increase bleeding risk. Talk to your doctor if you take blood thinners or have surgery planned. It may also interact with some HIV and blood pressure medicines.

why: A traditional tonic used to support immune health.*

caution: Avoid if you take immunosuppressants or have had a transplant, and check with your doctor if you have an autoimmune condition. May interact with blood thinners, blood pressure and diabetes medicines.

name: Elderberry Syrup
what: A syrup or gummy made from cooked black elderberries (Sambucus nigra).
why: Supports immune health in cold and flu season. May help colds feel shorter and milder.*

evidence.note: A 2021 systematic review of five trials found elderberry may reduce the length and severity of colds, but called the evidence uncertain. It probably does not stop you catching one.

caution: Never eat raw or unripe elderberries, which can cause nausea and vomiting. Not recommended in pregnancy for lack of safety data. Ask your doctor if you take immunosuppressants or diabetes medicine.

name: Echinacea
what: A flowering herb taken as tea, tincture or capsules.
why: Supports the body's natural defenses at the first sign of a cold.*

evidence.note: A Cochrane review of 24 trials found weak evidence overall. Pooled results suggest a small (10 to 20%) drop in the chance of catching a cold, of uncertain importance. Products vary a lot.

caution: Can cause allergic reactions, especially if you are allergic to ragweed, daisies or marigolds. Check with your doctor if you have an autoimmune condition or take immunosuppressants.

name: Zinc Lozenges
what: Lozenges made with zinc acetate or zinc gluconate that dissolve slowly in the mouth.
why: Taken at the first sign of a cold. May help shorten colds.*

evidence.note: A 2024 Cochrane review found zinc may shorten a cold by about two days, with low-certainty evidence. A separate reanalysis of lozenge trials found a larger effect. Start within 24 hours of symptoms.

caution: Can cause nausea and a bad taste. Use for a few days only, and stay under 40 mg of zinc a day long term. Avoid zinc nasal sprays, which have been linked to loss of smell. Space it apart from antibiotics.

name: Raw Honey
what: Unprocessed honey, taken by the spoonful or stirred into warm tea.
why: Soothes the throat and helps calm a nighttime cough.*

evidence.note: A Cochrane review found honey probably eases cough in children more than no treatment or placebo. Evidence quality was low to moderate, and most studies lasted one night.

caution: Never give honey to babies under 12 months because of the risk of infant botulism. Honey is sugar, so count it if you have diabetes.

what: A squeeze bottle or neti pot used to rinse the nose with salt water.
why: Rinses out mucus and helps you breathe more comfortably when stuffed up.*

evidence.note: A Cochrane review of five trials found saline rinsing is safe and possibly eases symptoms, but the evidence is limited.

caution: Use only distilled, sterile or previously boiled and cooled water. Never use plain tap water, which can carry organisms that cause rare but serious infections. Clean and dry the bottle after every use.

what: A drink mix with sodium, potassium and other minerals, often with a little glucose.
why: Supports hydration when you are sweating, not eating well or losing fluids.*

evidence.note: Oral rehydration solutions are one of the best-studied tools in medicine. Cochrane reviews find they rehydrate about as well as IV fluids in most cases.

caution: Check with your doctor first if you have kidney disease, heart failure or high blood pressure, or take diuretics or potassium-sparing medicines. Watch the sugar and sodium on the label.

name: Bone Broth
what: A slow-simmered broth, sold ready to drink or as a powder.
why: A warm, easy-to-digest source of fluids, protein and salt when your appetite is low.

evidence.note: A well-known lab study found chicken soup slowed the movement of certain immune cells in a test tube. There are no good human trials, but warm fluids are a time-honored comfort.
evidence.label: Traditional use

caution: Often high in sodium, so check the label if you watch your salt. Long-simmered broths are high in histamine, which bothers some people.

why: Coats and soothes the throat.*

evidence.note: One randomized trial of 60 adults found a tea of this type eased throat discomfort better than placebo for about 30 minutes after drinking.

caution: Licorice root can raise blood pressure and lower potassium with regular use. Avoid if you are pregnant or have high blood pressure, heart or kidney disease. Slippery elm may slow the absorption of medicines, so take them an hour apart.

what: Magnesium sulfate crystals that dissolve in a warm bath.
why: A warm soak people use to relax and ease tired, achy muscles.

evidence.note: A long-standing home tradition. A 2017 review found little evidence that magnesium is absorbed through the skin, so the comfort likely comes from the warm bath itself.
evidence.label: Traditional use

caution: For soaking only. Do not drink it unless a doctor tells you to. Skip hot baths if you have a fever, feel dizzy or have open wounds. Ask your doctor first if you have kidney disease.

name: Probiotics
what: Capsules of live beneficial bacteria, usually Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains.
why: Support a healthy balance of gut bacteria, including during and after antibiotics.*

evidence.note: Cochrane reviews find probiotics are likely to lower the number of upper respiratory infections and help keep digestion regular during antibiotic use. Effects depend on the strain.

caution: Not for people with weakened immune systems, serious illness or a central line, or for premature infants, unless a doctor approves. May cause gas or bloating at first.

why: Supports regularity and feeds beneficial gut bacteria.*

caution: Always take with a full glass of water, as it can swell and cause choking if taken dry. Take medicines 2 hours apart. Not for people with trouble swallowing or a bowel obstruction.

caution: Raw, unpasteurized ferments are not recommended if you have a weakened immune system. They are high in salt and histamine, which bothers some people.

evidence.note: A review of three small trials in older adults found magnesium helped people fall asleep about 17 minutes faster, but the evidence quality was low.

caution: Ask your doctor first if you have kidney disease. Take it 2 hours apart from antibiotics and osteoporosis medicines. The upper limit from supplements is 350 mg a day. Too much causes loose stools.
